plan.analysis: Only evidence so far: the constant seed gives R=2/3 (triangular autoconvolution). Main structural bet: f(x) ∝ x^{-1/2} has f*f exactly constant on [0,1], i.e. a flat plateau at the maximum over half the support, so its R is far above 2/3 (~0.89 even unoptimized). I bet on this power-law basin plus resolution: the singular first cell needs large N. Three experiments: (1) power-law seed + log-domain stochastic hill climb at N=2000; (2) coarse-to-fine hill climb from the constant start as a control for how much the seed matters; (3) the same optimizer at N=20000 to measure whether more steps raise R. All judged by the returned score.

experiments.hypothesis: h_i=(i+0.5)^-0.5 makes f*f flat on [0,1] and gives R near 0.89; local improvement of the tail should push it higher, well above 2/3.
experiments.change: Build construct(budget,start) ignoring start: N=2000, initial h[i]=(i+0.5)**-0.5, u=log(h). Score exactly as spec: L=concat([0],convolve(h,h),[0]); T=h.sum(); M=L.max(); S=sum(L[j]^2+L[j]L[j+1]+L[j+1]^2)/3 over consecutive knots; R=S/(M*T*T). Loop until time.process_time() nears budget-0.5s: with prob 0.7 perturb one random u[i] by delta~N(0,eps), else perturb a random contiguous block of length k=random 1..N/20 by the same delta; accept if R rises, else revert. Adapt eps: accepted -> eps*=1.02 (cap 0.5); rejected -> eps*=0.999; if no accept in 200 trials, eps=max(0.7*eps,1e-4), and every 20000 trials reset eps=0.05. Keep and return best h seen.
experiments.prediction: Returned R >= 0.90 at N=2000 (pure power law already ~0.89), far above 0.6667.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: rerun this basin at N=50000-200000 with longer time, and add a tail-focused optimizer (target near-maximum knots); also seed the coarse-to-fine program with this construction.
experiments.if_not: If R<0.80 the hill climber is faulty or the basin underperforms; fall back to coarse-to-fine search and test a target-flatness (deconvolution-style) update instead.

experiments.hypothesis: Plain stochastic ascent from the constant start, refined across resolutions (64,256,1024,4096), finds a good shape without the power-law prior and shows how much the seed matters.
experiments.change: Same exact scoring and log-domain hill-climb loop as the first experiment, but with a schedule: resample `start` (constant length 50) to N=64 by np.interp over step centers, optimize for 15% of budget, upsample the best h to N=256 (np.interp), optimize 20%, then N=1024 (25%), then N=4096 (40%); rescale each upsampled h to have sum equal to the previous best's sum before continuing. Return best h. Use time.process_time and stop at budget-0.5s.
experiments.prediction: R around 0.82-0.87, clearly below the power-law-seeded run; R rises with N within the run.
experiments.if_gain: Keep as the generic optimizer and, if it approaches the power-law run, combine: feed the power-law construction into this schedule as an alternative start each generation.
experiments.if_not: If it stalls near 0.70-0.75, stochastic coordinate ascent is too weak; switch to gradient-based ascent with a smoothed max in the next generation.

plan.analysis: Record 0.8808 comes from the power-law seed; raising N 2000→20000 gave only +0.003, so the grid is not binding — the plateau shape and the weak random-block hill climber are. Since R ≈ plateau/(plateau+tail) for a flat-topped f*f, gains must come from a seed whose f*f drops faster, or from a much stronger local optimizer. Previous work: plain coarse-to-fine from the constant start only reached 0.806; power-law seed dominates. I bet on three distinct, cheap-to-test moves this generation: (1) scan genuinely different seed families (spike+bang-bang, two-sided beta singularities) that may put f*f closer to bang-bang; (2) a finite-difference L-BFGS ascent in log-height at coarse N then upsample; (3) a deterministic multiscale block-scaling sweep using FFT convolution so thousands of systematic moves fit in the budget.

experiments.hypothesis: The power-law seed is one point in a family; seeds whose f*f is closer to bang-bang (flat with a steeper right edge) have less tail mass for the same plateau and thus strictly higher R than 0.8808.
experiments.change: Keep the exact score function and the returned-best logic. At N=1200 build and score these seed families (exact R, no hill climb yet): (a) h_i=(i+0.5)^-a * (N-i-0.5)^-b for a,b in {0,0.25,0.5,0.75} (skip a=b=0, clamp exponents); (b) spike+bang-bang h_0=c, h_i=1 for i<M, h_i=1e-3 otherwise, c in {1,3,10,30,100}, M in {N/8,N/4,N/2,3N/4}; (c) power-law with a right-edge spike h_i=(i+0.5)^-0.5 + c*exp(-(N-1-i)/tau) for c in {0.5,2,10}, tau in {5,20,80}. Take the top 5 seeds by exact R, run 400 random log-domain block perturbations on each (same accept/keep-best rule), then take the overall best, upsample it to N=8000 and do 400 more perturbations. Print each family's best R and the final R. Return the best construction seen.
experiments.prediction: At least one non-power-law family (probably spike+bang-bang or two-sided beta) scores above 0.881 after its short climb, i.e. a new basin better than the power-law seed; if all families stay below 0.875 the power-law basin is special.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: take the winning family and optimize it at N=50000 with a long dedicated run, and grid its remaining free parameters finely.
experiments.if_not: Drop seed hunting; the power-law basin is confirmed special, so spend next generation entirely on stronger optimizers around the current best shape.

experiments.kind: finite-difference L-BFGS ascent in log-height, coarse-to-fine
experiments.hypothesis: The record's optimizer accepts only single random moves; a quasi-Newton method using finite-difference gradients of R in log-height coordinates at coarse N will find a better local optimum of the same shape, and upsampling plus a short climb will carry it above 0.8808.
experiments.change: Use scipy.optimize.minimize(method='L-BFGS-B', jac=None (2-point finite differences), bounds on u=log h in [-25,25]). Objective is -R with the exact scorer (use scipy.signal.fftconvolve instead of np.convolve for speed; same formula). Schedule by CPU time: first 40% of budget at N=120 from a resampled best start, next 30% at N=350 (upsample the best u by linear interpolation of h), final 30% at N=1200. After each stage, evaluate exact R, keep the global best h, and call keep_best. At the end upsample the best to N=20000 and run the original random block hill climb for whatever time remains, returning the best seen. Print each stage's N and R.
experiments.prediction: The stage-R sequence rises and the final returned R exceeds 0.8808 (gradient information finds a genuinely better shape than random blocks); if the coarse-R plateaus at ~0.87 upsampling may still not beat the record.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: switch to an exact adjoint/analytic gradient of R through the convolution (O(N log N) per step) and run full quasi-Newton at N=20000.
experiments.if_not: Conclude finite-difference gradients at coarse N lose too much resolution; keep the random climber but give it a systematically chosen move set instead.

experiments.kind: deterministic multiscale block-scaling sweep with FFT convolution
experiments.hypothesis: Random single blocks rarely improve a flat plateau; a deterministic sweep that tries a grid of scaling factors on every block at every scale will accumulate many small accepted improvements on the existing best shape and beat 0.8808.
experiments.change: Keep the exact score formula but implement it with scipy.signal.fftconvolve for speed (same L, S, T, M). Start from the resampled best construction at N=20000, u=log h. Loop over scales in this order and repeat the whole schedule until 92% of budget: for block length k in [N//8, N//32, N//128, N//512, 1], for each consecutive block of length k (step k), try u_block += d for d in [+0.3,-0.3,+0.1,-0.1,+0.03,-0.03,+0.01,-0.01,+0.003,-0.003]; accept the first d that raises exact R, otherwise revert and move on. After each full pass print pass number, scale reached, current best R. Always keep and return the global best h via keep_best when improved.
experiments.prediction: Several full passes complete and the returned R exceeds 0.8808 by a visible margin (e.g. ≥0.882), showing the random climber was leaving deterministic slack on the table.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: couple this sweep as the inner loop of the p0003 optimizer and add a tail-only fine sweep (last 15% of the support) plus a plateau-edge alignment move.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the shape is at a strong local optimum and switch to changing the seed family or objective (e.g. explicitly minimizing tail mass at fixed plateau).

plan.analysis: The record (0.880865) is still well below the continuous x^-1/2 construction (~0.889 by direct computation), so the gap is likely a mix of finite-N resolution and a non-flat second half of f*f. Local random moves have saturated. I am betting on three distinct moves: (1) an exact analytic-gradient L-BFGS ascent using a smooth p-norm max, which can reshape the whole plateau/tail rather than one coordinate at a time; (2) a high-resolution N=200000 run seeded by the exact discrete flat-half sequence h_k=C(2k,k)/4^k, which makes f*f exactly constant on the first half and directly tests whether discretization near the singular endpoint is the remaining bottleneck; (3) a systematic global log-tilt/right-edge mass scan, which tests whether local search has missed the right global balance between the left singularity and the second-half tail.

experiments.hypothesis: The current random coordinate/block climber cannot efficiently flatten the whole f*f plateau or raise the second-half tail. An exact-gradient quasi-Newton method in log-height, using a smooth p-norm replacement for the maximum, will find a better shape by moving many heights coherently.
experiments.change: Replace p0012's random hillclimb with an exact-gradient L-BFGS-B ascent in u=log(h) at N=20000. Use scipy.signal.fftconvolve to compute L=conv(h,h) with the same zero padding as score. For fixed p compute M_p=(sum_j L_j^p)^(1/p), S=sum_j (L_j^2+L_j L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2)/3, T=sum h. Implement gradients: dS/dL_j=(L_{j-1}+4L_j+L_{j+1})/3 with zero outside; dM_p/dL_j=L_j^(p-1)/M_p^(p-1). Then dS/dh and dM_p/dh are obtained by convolving h with these L-space derivative arrays (the derivative of L_j=sum h_a h_{j-a} is 2h_{j-i}); chain to u by multiplying by h. Objective = S/(T^2 M_p). Warm-start L-BFGS-B through p=8,16,32,64, with u bounds [-30,30], using time.process_time() and stopping before a 2 s margin. After every p stage score the true h with score(h) and keep_best. Start from the provided best construction.
experiments.prediction: The p-norm objective decreases and the returned true R exceeds 0.880865 by at least 0.0005, showing coherent gradient reshaping beats coordinate moves.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: run the same analytic-gradient method at N=50000 or 200000, and use the p-norm shape as the new start for further local polishing.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the current plateau/tail balance is already a strong local optimum under smooth objectives; shift entirely to structural seeds and high-resolution discretization.

experiments.kind: high-resolution exact binomial seed + local polish
experiments.hypothesis: The continuous x^-1/2 construction scores about 0.889, so the N=20000 optimum is limited by finite-step resolution near the singular endpoint. The exact discrete analog h_k=C(2k,k)/4^k makes conv(h,h) exactly constant on the entire first half; at N=200000 its boundary layer is finer and should score above the current record.
experiments.change: Ignore the supplied start. Set N=200000 and build h[0]=1, h[k]=h[k-1]*(2*k-1)/(2*k) for k=1..N-1 (this is C(2k,k)/4^k). Score and keep it; print the init score. Then spend the remaining time on a limited log-domain local polish: use score(h) (or an exact fftconvolve implementation) and try block moves of size N//500 plus single-coordinate moves, accepting only improvements, with small steps eps in [0.005,0.05]. Bias move locations toward the second half and last 10% of indices so the tail can be flattened. Keep the best array anywhere and return it, leaving at least 1 s margin.
experiments.prediction: The binomial seed alone is at or above 0.8810, and the short polish pushes it to at least 0.8820, confirming that finite-N discretization was still binding.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: combine this high-N construction with the analytic-gradient method and optimize the right-half tail systematically.
experiments.if_not: Conclude N=20000 is already effectively converged and high resolution alone will not close the gap; focus on changing the shape family/tail construction.

experiments.hypothesis: Local moves may not change the global balance of mass between the left singular region and the right side. A systematic multiplicative tilt and right-edge boost will test whether the current second-half convolution is too low; the best tilted candidate plus local repair can raise R.
experiments.change: Start from the provided best h at N=20000. For a grid of a in {-0.5,-0.4,...,0.5} and b in {0,0.25,0.5,1.0}, form h' = h * exp(a*(2*i/(N-1)-1)) * (1 + b*exp(-(N-1-i)/(0.08*N))). Evaluate score(h') for every grid point (keeping the a=b=0 candidate equal to h), and keep the best candidate. Then run p0012's existing coordinate/block hill climb from that best tilted candidate for the remaining time, always keeping the global best found. Print the best grid candidate score and the final score.
experiments.prediction: At least one nonzero tilt/boost candidate scores above 0.880865, and local repair from it reaches at least 0.8810, showing the global mass distribution was suboptimal.
experiments.if_gain: Next generation: replace the two-parameter tilt with a piecewise-linear or spline envelope over i/N and optimize its knots; combine with the analytic gradient.
experiments.if_not: Conclude the current global mass distribution is locally and globally well balanced for this shape family; prioritize high-resolution and gradient methods over envelope searches.
